course.title: Business Model Design
course.description: A plain-language introduction to how businesses actually work - what a business model is, the nine blocks of the Business Model Canvas, the Value Proposition Canvas, revenue models, and the patterns that recur across successful companies. You will learn to map, test, and iterate a model and to see how it connects to strategy, following the framework associated with Alexander Osterwalder. Structure and terminology adapted from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: A business model mainly describes:
options: how a company creates, delivers, and captures value
the company logo and brand colors
the number of employees on the payroll
questions.explanation: A business model is the logic of value creation, delivery, and capture - not just the product or the branding.

questions.prompt: The Business Model Canvas is made up of how many building blocks?
questions.explanation: The canvas has nine blocks - see the lesson on the Business Model Canvas.

questions.prompt: Which revenue model gives a basic version away free and charges for premium features?
questions.explanation: Freemium offers a free tier and earns from the share of users who upgrade.

questions.prompt: In an advertising-supported model, who typically pays?
options: the user who gets the content
questions.explanation: The user gets value for free while the advertiser pays for their attention - payer and user differ.

questions.prompt: A marketplace business earns money mainly by:
options: manufacturing all of its own goods
taking a commission on transactions between two groups
questions.explanation: A marketplace matches two sides and takes a cut of the transactions it enables.

questions.prompt: The Value Proposition Canvas focuses on the fit between:
options: customer needs and what you offer
questions.explanation: It matches the customer profile (jobs, pains, gains) to your value map.

questions.prompt: Treating a business model as a set of guesses to check is best described as:
questions.explanation: Strong teams test risky assumptions with small, fast experiments.

questions.prompt: Which pair are both blocks of the Business Model Canvas?
questions.explanation: Key activities and cost structure are two of the nine canvas blocks.

lessons.title: What a business model is
lessons.grammar_note: A business model and a strategy are not the same thing: strategy picks where to compete, while the business model is the operating logic that earns money day to day.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what a business model actually is, tell it apart from a product idea and from a strategy, and describe the simple logic by which any organization creates value, delivers that value to people, and captures some of it in return. By the end you will be able to look at a company you already use and state, in one or two sentences, who it serves and how it earns money. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, pick one business you interacted with this week and answer three questions out loud - who is the customer, what problem is being solved, and where does the money come from? Keep that example in mind, because every idea in this course will attach to a concrete business rather than to a bare definition. Having a real company on the table makes each new term easier to pin down and far harder to fake.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A business model is the story of how an organization creates value for customers, delivers that value, and captures part of it as revenue. Put simply, it answers three questions - what do we offer, to whom, and how do we get paid? A product is only one piece of that story; a great product with no way to reach customers or charge for the work is not yet a business. Strategy sits one level up: strategy is the set of choices a company makes to compete and win in its market, while the business model is the operating logic that turns those choices into a working, money-making system. The two are tightly linked. A clear strategy tells you which customers to chase and which to ignore; the business model shows the machinery that serves them profitably. People often summarize a model in a single sentence: we help a certain customer do a certain job through a certain offer, and we earn money through a certain revenue source. If you cannot fill in that sentence, the model is not yet clear.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Consider three familiar businesses. A neighborhood bakery creates value by baking fresh bread, delivers it over a counter, and captures value through one-time cash sales; its model is simple and old. A streaming service creates value by licensing a large catalog of shows, delivers it over the internet to any screen, and captures value through a monthly subscription that renews on its own. A search website creates value by answering questions for free, delivers results instantly, and captures value by selling advertising space to businesses that want attention from those searchers - here the user and the payer are different people, which is worth noticing. Each example shows the same three-part logic with different wiring. Value creation can be a physical good, a service, access, or information. Delivery can be a shop, a fleet, an app, or a website. Value capture can be a price per unit, a recurring fee, a commission, or advertising. Alexander Osterwalder, whose work anchors this course, argues that writing the model down on a single shared page keeps a team honest about all three parts at once.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Fill in the sentence for a coffee shop: we help ___ do ___ by ___, and we earn money through ___. 2) State the difference between a product and a business model. 3) A free mobile game earns money from a small share of players who buy extras - who is the customer, and who is the payer? 4) Is 'sell more than competitors' a strategy or a business model? 5) Give one way a bakery could capture value other than one-time sales. Answers: 1) Example - we help busy commuters get a quick caffeine fix by serving fast espresso near the station, and we earn money through per-cup sales. 2) A product is one thing you offer; the business model is the whole logic of creating, delivering, and capturing value around it. 3) The customer is every player who gets value; the payer is the small group who buy extras. 4) A strategy - it is a competitive choice, not the operating logic of earning. 5) A monthly bread subscription, catering contracts, or selling branded goods.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing the product with the business model - a clever feature is not a model until you can say who pays and why. Mistake: treating 'make money' as the whole answer; a model must name the customer and the value before the revenue makes any sense. Mistake: mixing up strategy and model, then arguing in circles; remember that strategy picks the game while the model runs the machine. Exit: (a) What three things does every business model describe? (b) In an advertising model, who can differ - the customer who gets value or the one who pays? Answers: how it creates value, how it delivers value, and how it captures value as revenue; the payer can differ from the user, since advertisers pay for the attention that users supply for free.

lessons.title: The Business Model Canvas and its nine blocks
lessons.grammar_note: Key resources are assets you hold (licenses, servers); key activities are things you do (licensing, streaming) - keep the two blocks apart.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Draw the Business Model Canvas from memory and name all nine building blocks, then place real facts about a company into the right block. You will be able to use the canvas as a shared map that a whole team can read at a glance, instead of a long written plan that no one keeps up to date. By the end you should be able to sketch nine empty boxes on a napkin and fill them for any business you know well. Warm-up: before reading on, try to list from the diagnostic any three things a company needs besides a product in order to operate - for example, people who buy, a way to reach them, and money coming in. Hold those guesses, because several of them are canvas blocks already, and spotting them now will make the full list feel less like memorization and more like naming things you had half-noticed on your own.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Business Model Canvas, created by Alexander Osterwalder, is a single page divided into nine blocks that together describe how an organization works. On the right sit the blocks that face the customer: customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, and revenue streams. On the left sit the blocks that make the offer possible behind the scenes: key resources, key activities, key partnerships, and cost structure. The idea is that a business model is not a long document but a picture you can see and argue about together. Because the whole model fits on one page, a team can spot gaps fast - for instance, a strong value proposition with no channel to reach the customer, or heavy costs with no matching revenue stream. The canvas does not tell you whether a model is good; it forces you to make every part explicit so you can test it. Think of the right side as the promise to the market and the left side as the engine that keeps the promise, with revenue and cost at the bottom showing whether the engine pays for itself.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Here are the nine blocks, with a streaming service as the running example. 1) Customer segments - the distinct groups you serve; here, households that watch shows at home. 2) Value propositions - the bundle of value you offer; a large catalog watchable any time without advertisements. 3) Channels - how you reach and deliver; apps on phones, televisions, and browsers. 4) Customer relationships - the kind of tie you keep; self-service with automatic recommendations. 5) Revenue streams - how you earn; a flat monthly subscription. 6) Key resources - the assets you must have; content licenses, servers, and the brand. 7) Key activities - the critical things you do; licensing and producing shows and running reliable streaming. 8) Key partnerships - outside help you depend on; studios, internet providers, and device makers. 9) Cost structure - your main costs; content spending and infrastructure. Read the right side as the customer promise and the left as the engine. Osterwalder's point is that all nine must fit together, not merely each be strong on its own.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which side of the canvas holds channels, left or right? 2) Into which block does 'monthly subscription fee' go? 3) Name the block for 'the studios that license us their films.' 4) A gym lists 'trainers and the building' - which block? 5) True or false: the canvas tells you if your model will succeed. 6) Which two blocks sit at the very bottom and show whether the engine pays for itself? Answers: 1) Right - it faces the customer. 2) Revenue streams. 3) Key partnerships. 4) Key resources. 5) False - it makes the model explicit so you can test it, but it does not judge it for you. 6) Cost structure on the left and revenue streams on the right.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: filling only the right side and forgetting the engine - a loved offer with no key resources or partners will not run. Mistake: confusing key resources (assets you own or hold, like licenses and servers) with key activities (things you do, like licensing and streaming). Mistake: listing every possible customer instead of naming distinct segments with different needs. Exit: (a) How many blocks does the canvas have, and which four sit on the left? (b) Which block names the groups you serve? Answers: nine blocks; the left holds key resources, key activities, key partnerships, and cost structure; customer segments names the groups you serve.

lessons.title: The Value Proposition Canvas
lessons.grammar_note: A gain is an outcome the customer wants; a gain creator is the part of your offer that produces it - do not blur the two.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Use the Value Proposition Canvas to zoom in on the fit between what customers want and what you offer. You will be able to list a customer's jobs, pains, and gains, then design products, pain relievers, and gain creators that match them. By the end you will be able to explain why a feature list is not the same as a value proposition, and what people really mean by the phrase product-market fit. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, think of a product you bought and were disappointed by - which promise did it fail to keep? That gap between promise and need is exactly what this tool is built to close. Keep that letdown in mind as a test case; by the end of the lesson you should be able to say which pain the product ignored or which gain it never delivered, in the tool's own vocabulary.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The Value Proposition Canvas, also from Alexander Osterwalder, zooms into two blocks of the larger canvas - value propositions and customer segments - and asks whether they truly fit. It has two halves. The customer profile, drawn as a circle, lists three things: customer jobs (what the customer is trying to get done, in work or life), pains (the annoyances, risks, and obstacles they face), and gains (the outcomes and benefits they want). The value map, drawn as a square, also lists three things: products and services you offer, pain relievers (how your offer removes specific pains), and gain creators (how it produces the gains the customer wants). Fit happens when your pain relievers and gain creators line up with the customer's most important pains and gains - not with every pain, only the ones that matter. The tool stops teams from building features nobody asked for. Instead of starting from what is easy to build, you start from the customer's real jobs and design backward. When the map matches the profile on the points that count, you have the beginnings of product-market fit.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Take a small accounting app for freelancers. Customer profile first. Jobs: send invoices, track expenses, file taxes on time. Pains: dreading tax season, losing receipts, wasting evenings on spreadsheets. Gains: feeling in control, paying the right tax, getting weekends back. Now the value map. Products and services: an invoicing tool, a receipt scanner, an automatic tax estimate. Pain relievers: the scanner ends lost receipts; the estimate removes tax-season dread; templates cut the evening spreadsheet work. Gain creators: a clear dashboard gives a feeling of control; reminders mean deadlines are met. Notice the discipline - each reliever points at a named pain, and each creator points at a named gain. A feature with no matching pain or gain is a candidate to cut. Osterwalder's rule of thumb is to rank the customer's jobs, pains, and gains by importance first, then check whether your strongest relievers and creators address the top of that list. If your best features only touch minor pains, the fit is weak even when the product is polished.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) In the customer profile, what are the three lists? 2) In the value map, what are the three lists? 3) Classify 'I keep losing receipts' - job, pain, or gain? 4) Classify 'a receipt scanner that saves every photo' - product, pain reliever, or gain creator? 5) Why rank jobs, pains, and gains before designing? Answers: 1) Jobs, pains, and gains. 2) Products and services, pain relievers, and gain creators. 3) A pain. 4) A product or service, which here also acts as a pain reliever for lost receipts. 5) So your strongest relievers and creators address the pains and gains that matter most, instead of minor ones that will not move a buyer.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: listing features before understanding the customer's jobs, which leads to polished products nobody needs. Mistake: trying to relieve every pain instead of the few that matter most. Mistake: confusing a gain (an outcome the customer wants) with a gain creator (the part of your offer that produces it). Exit: (a) Which two blocks of the Business Model Canvas does the Value Proposition Canvas zoom into? (b) What word describes a strong match between the value map and the customer profile? Answers: value propositions and customer segments; fit, which is the seed of product-market fit. Remember that fit is judged on the customer's most important points, not on the length of your feature list.

questions.prompt: A business model describes how an organization creates value, delivers it, and:
options: captures part of it as revenue
questions.explanation: The three-part logic is create, deliver, and capture value.

questions.prompt: Which blocks sit on the customer-facing right side of the canvas?
questions.explanation: The right side faces the customer: segments, value propositions, channels, relationships, and revenue streams.

questions.prompt: 'The studios that license us films' belongs in which canvas block?
questions.explanation: Outside parties you depend on go in key partnerships.

questions.prompt: In the Value Proposition Canvas, jobs, pains, and gains describe:
questions.explanation: Jobs, pains, and gains make up the customer profile half of the tool.

questions.prompt: A pain reliever should be designed to address:
questions.explanation: Fit comes from matching the pains and gains that matter most.

questions.prompt: Who created the Business Model Canvas and the Value Proposition Canvas?
questions.explanation: Both tools are associated with Alexander Osterwalder.

lessons.title: Revenue models: how a business gets paid
lessons.grammar_note: Not every recurring charge is a subscription: usage-based billing rises and falls with how much the customer consumes.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name and compare the main ways a business can earn money, and pick a revenue model that fits a given offer and customer. You will be able to tell a one-time sale from a subscription, explain why freemium can work, and spot when advertising or licensing makes sense. By the end you should be able to argue for one revenue model over another for a specific product, not just define the terms. Warm-up: list every business you paid this month and, beside each, write how you paid - once, monthly, by usage, or not at all because someone else paid. That quick audit previews every model in this lesson, and the one you wrote 'not at all' next to is probably an advertising model in disguise, which is the case most people get wrong when they first meet it.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A revenue model is the specific way a business captures value - it fills the revenue streams block of the canvas. Six patterns cover most cases. One-time sales charge a price each time the customer buys, like a bakery or a furniture shop; revenue is lumpy and you must keep finding buyers. Subscription charges a recurring fee for ongoing access, like a streaming service or a magazine; revenue is predictable but you must keep earning each renewal. Freemium gives a basic version free and charges for premium features, counting on a small share of free users to upgrade; it trades low barriers to entry against the cost of serving many non-payers. Usage-based, or pay-as-you-go, charges in proportion to how much the customer uses, like a cloud host billing by the hour or a utility by the kilowatt-hour. Advertising offers something free to users and sells their attention to advertisers, so the user and the payer differ. Licensing charges others for the right to use your intellectual property, such as a song, a patent, or a brand. Many real businesses blend two or more of these rather than relying on a single one.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Match the model to the offer. A clothing shop uses one-time sales because each purchase is a discrete event. A music service uses a subscription because listeners want continuous access and the catalog keeps costing money to license. A note-taking app uses freemium: anyone can start free, and heavy users pay for extra storage and sharing, so the free tier is really the marketing. A cloud database uses usage-based pricing because its costs scale with how much customers store and query, so billing by usage keeps the vendor's margin steady. A free news website uses advertising because readers will not pay but advertisers will pay for their attention. A chip designer uses licensing: it does not build phones, it licenses its designs to the companies that do, collecting a fee per device. Now blend them - a streaming service may run a cheaper advertisement-supported plan beside its paid subscription, capturing both the people who will pay and the people who will only watch for free. When you choose, ask how often value is delivered, how predictable you need revenue to be, and who is actually willing to pay.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name the revenue model: pay a fixed fee every month for access. 2) Name the model: a free tier plus paid premium features. 3) A cloud host bills by the gigabyte stored - which model? 4) A free puzzle website earns from banner ads - who is the payer? 5) A patent holder earns a fee each time another firm uses its invention - which model? 6) Give one reason a company might blend subscription and advertising. Answers: 1) Subscription. 2) Freemium. 3) Usage-based. 4) The advertisers, not the puzzle players. 5) Licensing. 6) To capture both willing payers and free users, widening the audience while still earning from those who will not pay directly.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling every recurring charge a subscription when usage-based billing rises and falls with consumption. Mistake: assuming freemium is free money - every non-paying user still costs something to serve, so the paid upgrades must cover them. Mistake: forgetting that in advertising the user and the payer are different people, which shapes every design choice. Exit: (a) Which model gives the most predictable revenue, and which is the lumpiest? (b) In freemium, where does the revenue actually come from? Answers: subscription is the most predictable and one-time sales the lumpiest; the revenue comes from the small share of users who upgrade to the paid tier.

lessons.title: Common business model patterns
lessons.grammar_note: Name a pattern by its underlying logic, not by the brand, since one company can run several patterns at once.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Recognize four recurring business model patterns - marketplace, razor-and-blades, long tail, and platform - and explain the logic that makes each one work. You will be able to name the pattern behind a familiar company and say what makes it hard to copy. By the end you should be able to sketch, for each pattern, who benefits, who pays, and why the pattern defends itself against competitors. Warm-up: think of an app that connects two different groups of people, such as drivers and riders or hosts and guests. That connecting trick is one of the four patterns, and you already use it. Try to say aloud, before reading on, why it would be hard for a brand-new copy of that app to steal its users even if the copy looked identical - your answer is the heart of this lesson.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Business model patterns are proven shapes that many successful companies reuse. A marketplace connects two groups - buyers and sellers, riders and drivers, guests and hosts - and earns a commission on the transactions it enables; its power comes from network effects, since more sellers attract more buyers and the other way around, which makes a busy marketplace hard to unseat. Razor-and-blades sells a core product cheaply, sometimes at a loss, then earns steady profit on the consumables it requires - the printer and its ink, the console and its games, the coffee machine and its pods. The long tail earns money not from a few blockbusters but from an enormous catalog of niche items, each selling rarely, which only works when storage and distribution are cheap enough to stock everything. A platform provides the ground on which others build and trade - an app store, an operating system, a payment network - and captures value as that ecosystem grows. These patterns are not rigid templates; they are lenses. Real companies often combine them, and the same firm can be a marketplace and a platform at once.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: See each pattern in the wild. Marketplace: an online auction site owns no inventory; it simply matches sellers with buyers and takes a cut, growing stronger as each side attracts the other. Razor-and-blades: a home espresso maker is sold at a slim margin, while the branded pods it needs are sold again and again at a healthy one, so the machine locks in future purchases. Long tail: a streaming catalog stocks millions of obscure tracks that each earn little, yet together these niche plays rival the hits, because digital storage costs almost nothing per extra title. Platform: a smartphone operating system lets outside developers publish apps, and the owner takes a share of sales while the growing library makes the phones more valuable - a self-reinforcing loop. Notice the defenses. The marketplace and the platform are guarded by network effects. Razor-and-blades is guarded by the tie between the base product and its consumables. The long tail is guarded by the sheer breadth of catalog and the data about which rare items to recommend. Patterns are starting points you adapt, not recipes you copy exactly.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which pattern connects two groups and earns a commission? 2) Selling a cheap console and profitable games is which pattern? 3) A bookstore that profits from millions of rarely bought titles uses which pattern? 4) What defends a marketplace from competitors? 5) Name one role that can be both a marketplace and a platform. Answers: 1) Marketplace. 2) Razor-and-blades. 3) The long tail. 4) Network effects - each side attracts the other, so a busy marketplace is hard to displace. 5) An app store, which both matches buyers with developers (a marketplace) and provides the ground others build on (a platform).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling any website with many products a long tail, when the long tail specifically earns from countless niche items rather than a few hits. Mistake: thinking a marketplace needs to own inventory - its job is to match two sides and take a commission. Mistake: treating patterns as rigid templates instead of lenses you adapt and combine. Exit: (a) What force protects both marketplaces and platforms? (b) In razor-and-blades, where does the steady profit come from? Answers: network effects; from the repeat sales of the consumable blades, not from the cheap razor. Remember that one real company may run several patterns at once, so name the pattern by its logic, not by the brand.

items.translation: the logic of how an organization creates value, delivers it to customers, and captures part of it as revenue
items.example: A streaming service and a bakery have very different business models even though both sell to the public.

items.translation: the bundle of value you offer a customer segment - the reason they choose you
items.example: The value proposition of a note-taking app might be fast capture of ideas on any device.

items.translation: a distinct group of people or organizations you aim to serve, with needs different from other groups
items.example: A gym may serve two segments - busy commuters at dawn and retirees at midday.

items.translation: a specific way a business earns money, such as a one-time sale, a subscription, or a commission
items.example: The company has two revenue streams: paid subscriptions and advertising on its free tier.

items.translation: a model that gives a basic version free and charges for premium features, earning from the few who upgrade
items.example: Under freemium, the free users act as marketing for the paid plan.

items.translation: the property that a product grows more valuable as more people use it, which defends marketplaces and platforms
items.example: A marketplace with many sellers attracts more buyers, whose demand then attracts yet more sellers - a network effect.

items.translation: a deliberate change of direction in the business model based on what a test taught you
items.example: When the price test failed, the team made a pivot and targeted larger families instead.

lessons.title: Testing, iterating, and the link to strategy
lessons.grammar_note: Test the riskiest assumption first; a failed cheap test is a saving, not a setback.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Treat a business model as a set of guesses to be tested, not a plan to be defended. You will be able to find the riskiest assumption in a model, design a cheap experiment to check it, and explain how a tested model feeds back into company strategy. By the end you should be able to describe a short build-measure-learn loop and say why strategy and the model must stay in conversation. Warm-up: look back at the canvas you imagined in the lesson on the nine blocks and circle the one block that, if it turned out to be wrong, would sink the whole thing. That block holds your riskiest assumption, and it is exactly where testing should start - not with the parts you are already confident about, which is where nervous teams tend to begin instead.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A new business model is a stack of assumptions, and most of them are unproven. The mistake is to write a long plan and execute it for a year before learning whether customers care. Instead, strong teams list their assumptions, rank them by risk, and test the riskiest ones first with small, fast experiments - a landing page, a few interviews, a single pilot sale. This loop is often called build, measure, learn: build the smallest thing that tests an assumption, measure what real people do, and learn whether to keep the guess or change it. Changing direction based on what you learn is called a pivot; keeping course is called persevere. Testing connects directly to strategy. Strategy is the set of choices about where to compete and how to win; the business model is how those choices operate day to day. When a test proves an assumption false - say, customers will not pay the planned price - that news should travel up to strategy, perhaps changing the target segment or the basis of competition. A model that is never tested lets a flawed strategy survive untouched until the money runs out.

sections.heading: Key concepts & examples
sections.text: Walk through a short loop. A team believes busy parents will pay for a weekly meal-kit subscription. The riskiest assumption is not whether they can cook the kits - it is whether parents will pay and keep paying. So before building a kitchen, they put up a simple page describing the kit and a price, drive a little traffic to it, and count how many click to pre-order. Few do. Rather than defend the idea, they interview the visitors and learn the price felt high for the portion size. They adjust the offer - larger portions, a small price cut - and test again; pre-orders climb. That is one build-measure-learn loop, and the adjustment was a small pivot in the value proposition and the revenue stream, two canvas blocks. Now connect it upward. The test revealed that the winning segment is larger families, not single parents - a strategy-level choice about who to serve. Osterwalder's canvas earns its keep here: because the whole model is visible on one page, the team can see exactly which block each experiment touches and how a change ripples into cost and revenue.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What are the three steps of the common test loop? 2) What is a pivot? 3) Which assumption should you test first - the easiest or the riskiest? 4) A price test fails badly - should that news reach strategy, or stay inside the model? 5) Name a cheap way to test whether people will pay before building the product. Answers: 1) Build, measure, learn. 2) A deliberate change of direction based on what a test taught you. 3) The riskiest, since it can sink the whole model. 4) It should reach strategy, which may change the target segment or how you compete. 5) A simple landing page with a price and a pre-order button, then count who clicks.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: testing the easy assumptions first and leaving the make-or-break one for last. Mistake: treating a failed test as a failure rather than as cheap learning that saved a costly mistake. Mistake: keeping strategy and the business model in separate conversations, so a disproven model never updates the plan. Exit: (a) What should you do with the riskiest assumption in a model? (b) When a test overturns an assumption, why must the result reach the strategy level? Answers: test it first, with the smallest and cheapest experiment that still gives a real signal; because strategy chose the customer and the way to compete, and new evidence may force a change in those choices, not only in the model's wiring.

questions.explanation: A recurring fee for continuing access is a subscription.

questions.explanation: A cheap base product plus profitable consumables is razor-and-blades.

questions.explanation: Each side attracts the other, so network effects protect a busy marketplace.

options: the small share of users who upgrade to paid

options: defend a plan for a year
test a model's assumptions cheaply and fast
